questions.q: Which gcc flag compiles simpleops.c into an IA32 (32-bit) executable?
questions.explain: The -m32 flag tells gcc to produce an IA32 executable, e.g. gcc -m32 -o simpleops simpleops.c.

questions.q: What is the benefit of adding -fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables when compiling with gcc -m32?
choices: It turns on optimizations so the program runs faster under GDB
It produces IA32 code that is a bit easier for a programmer to read and understand
It is required for GDB to set breakpoints on instruction addresses
It adds debugging symbols so GDB can show C source lines
questions.explain: This option is optional. It makes the generated IA32 code easier for a person to read.

questions.q: The GDB assembly-level commands (disass, si, ni, info registers, and so on) work only with IA32 assembly.
questions.explain: IA32 is just the example. The same GDB commands work with any assembly language that GCC supports.

questions.q: Type the GDB command that lists the assembly instructions of the function main (use the short form shown in the material).
questions.explain: disass <func_name> lists the assembly code for that function.

questions.q: Which GDB command sets a breakpoint at the single assembly instruction located at address 0x080483c1?
questions.explain: To break on an instruction address you dereference it with *: break *0x080483c1.

questions.q: What does the GDB command disass 0x1234 0x1248 do?
choices: Prints the memory contents from 0x1234 to 0x1248 as integers
Disassembles the function located at 0x1234 and the one at 0x1248
Lists the assembly instructions between addresses 0x1234 and 0x1248
questions.explain: disass <start> <end> lists the assembly instructions between the start and end addresses.

questions.q: The command break sum sets a breakpoint at the beginning of the function sum.
questions.explain: Giving a function name to break sets a breakpoint at the start of that function. Use break *ADDR to break on a specific instruction.

questions.q: The program is paused at a call instruction and you enter ni. Where does GDB pause next?
choices: At the first instruction of the called function
At the instruction after the call, once the called function has run and returned
At the next breakpoint, wherever it is
At the first instruction of main
questions.explain: ni (nexti) treats a function call as one instruction. It runs the whole call and pauses at the instruction right after it.

questions.q: The program is paused at a call instruction and you enter si. Where does GDB pause next?
choices: At the first instruction of the called function
At the instruction after the call, once the called function has run and returned
At the return instruction of the called function
It does not move, because si cannot step over a call
questions.explain: si (stepi) steps into function calls, so GDB pauses at the first instruction of the called function.

questions.q: Which statements about stepi/si and nexti/ni are true?
choices: si is short for stepi and ni is short for nexti
Both run the next machine code instruction
ni treats a function call as a single instruction
ni moves forward one line of C source code at a time
questions.explain: Both commands run one machine instruction. si steps into calls, and ni treats a call as a single instruction. Neither works by C source lines.

questions.q: What is the full name of the GDB command si?
questions.explain: si is the short form of stepi (step instruction).

questions.q: You are stopped at a breakpoint. Which command resumes normal execution until the next breakpoint?
questions.explain: cont continues running the program.

questions.q: In simpleops (x = 1; x = x + 2; x = x - 14; y = x * 100; x = x + y * 6;), you step through main one instruction at a time. What value does y hold once y = x * 100 has run?
questions.explain: x goes 1, then 3, then -11. So y = -11 * 100 = -1100.

questions.q: Using the same simpleops program, what value does x hold just before main returns?
questions.explain: Before the last statement x = -11 and y = -1100. Then x = -11 + (-1100 * 6) = -11 - 6600 = -6611.

questions.q: Which GDB command prints the value stored in register eax?
questions.explain: In GDB, register names start with $, so the command is print $eax (or p $eax).

questions.q: Which GDB command shows the values stored in all the machine registers?
questions.explain: info registers lists the contents of every register.

questions.q: How is display $eax different from print $eax?
choices: display shows eax automatically every time a breakpoint is hit, while print shows it only once
display shows eax in hexadecimal, while print shows it in decimal
display changes the value of eax, while print only reads it
display shows every register, while print shows only eax
questions.explain: display prints the expression each time a breakpoint is reached. print evaluates it only once.

questions.q: What does p *(int *)($ebp+8) print?
choices: The value of register ebp plus 8
The address ebp+8 shown as an int
The int value stored in memory at address (contents of ebp) + 8
The eighth int on the stack, counted from esp
questions.explain: $ebp+8 is computed as an address. It is cast to int * and dereferenced, so GDB prints the int stored there.

questions.q: What does the GDB command x $ebp-4 do?
choices: Prints the value of register ebp minus 4
Examines the memory at the address (contents of register ebp) - 4
Disassembles the instruction at address ebp - 4
questions.explain: x treats its argument as an address and shows the memory there. Here the address is ebp's value minus 4.

questions.q: Address 0x40062d holds the string "Hello There". Which command shows that memory as a string?
questions.explain: The /s format makes x show the memory as a string: 0x40062d "Hello There".

questions.q: The format used by the x command goes back to its default after every use, so you never need to reset the unit size.
questions.explain: The x format is sticky. A unit size set by an earlier command, such as 1 byte after x/4c or x/s, stays in effect until you change it.

questions.q: Address 0x40062d holds "Hello There". You run x/4c 0x40062d and get 72 'H' 101 'e' 108 'l' 108 'l'. If you then run x/d 0x40062d, what number is printed?
questions.explain: x/4c set the unit size to 1 byte, and that setting is sticky. So x/d reads 1 byte and prints 72 (the 'H').

questions.q: You just ran x/s on an address. Now you want to see a 4-byte int in decimal at 0xff5634. Which command is correct?
questions.explain: After x/s the unit size is 1 byte. You must give both the width w (4 bytes) and the format d.

questions.q: What is the effect of set $esp = $esp + 4 in GDB on IA32?
choices: It pushes a 4-byte value onto the stack
It stores 4 at the address in esp
It pops a 4-byte value off the stack
It prints the value 4 bytes above the stack pointer
questions.explain: Adding 4 to the stack pointer removes (pops) one 4-byte value from the stack.

questions.q: Which command stores the int 44 at memory address 0x8ff4bc10?
questions.explain: Cast the address to int * and dereference it, then use set to assign 44: set *(int *)0x8ff4bc10 = 44.

questions.q: Write the GDB command that sets register eax to 10.
questions.explain: set can change registers as well as memory: set $eax = 10.

questions.q: Which of these GDB commands move the program's execution forward?
questions.explain: ni, si, and cont all run the program. disass, info registers, and display only show information.

questions.q: What is DDD?
choices: A disassembler that replaces gcc's -m32 option
A graphical interface built on top of another debugger such as GDB
A command-line debugger that does not support GDB commands
A tool that converts assembly back into C source
questions.explain: DDD adds a graphical interface on top of a debugger like GDB, with windows for disassembled code, register values, and the GDB prompt.

questions.q: Write the shell command that starts DDD on the executable simpleops in the current directory.
questions.explain: To use DDD, type ddd in place of gdb: ddd ./simpleops.

questions.q: In DDD, which menu option opens a subwindow that shows the program's assembly code?
questions.explain: View -> Machine Code Window opens a subwindow listing the assembly code.

questions.q: In DDD, which menu option shows all of the program's register values in a separate window?
questions.explain: Turn on Status -> Registers to see the register values in their own window.

questions.q: In DDD, the bottom window holds a GDB prompt where you can type GDB commands directly.
questions.explain: DDD has buttons and menus for some commands, but the GDB prompt at the bottom is often easier to use.
